Dr. Roger Turner will present a talk highlighting the fascinating history of cultural practices and social groups on the field of spectroscopy, the scientific study of how matter interacts with electromagnetic radiation. His talk introduces some of the hidden figures who helped make spectroscopy a powerful technique that scientists use to understand the compositions of cultural heritage objects—including paintings, textiles, archeological artifacts, photographs, contemporary art, and much, much more. Women like Clara Smith Craver created the books of chemical “fingerprints” that identify different materials, while groups of scientists learned to how to do spectroscopy through summer courses at Fisk University, a historically Black university. Surprising objects from the Science History Institute museum reveal that spectroscopists can be playful and silly, while doing work that has transformed our understanding of art and archeology. Dr. Turner is the curator of instruments and artifacts at the Science History Institute in Philadelphia.

This is the keynote lecture for the IRUG Conference taking place at Winterthur October 7–9. IRUG is a group dedicated to the use of infrared and Raman spectroscopies applied to cultural heritage. Included with admission. Members free.

Bring in cherished objects and learn how to preserve them for future generations. Join conservators and conservation graduate students from the Winterthur/University of Delaware Program in Art Conservation for a hands-on workshop about how to care for your cherished objects in hazardous flood conditions. Participants will have the opportunity to learn a variety of processes from freezing and drying books to safely removing heavy, wet textiles from flood waters.

Offered in partnership with the University of Delaware’s Disaster Research Center, this workshop commemorates the 60th anniversary of the devastating 1966 Florence Flood. When Henry Francis du Pont purchased this portrait and installed it prominently in Montmorenci Stair Hall, it was identified simply as an “American Empire Portrait.” Yet it is not a mere likeness. This portrait of Catherine de Visme Browne by Ezra Ames depicts a young woman of great intellect, beauty, and ability, and also presents an embodiment of taste and moral character within the cultural aspirations of the nation. It offers an authoritative statement—first for the Browne family and later for du Pont—about cultural refinement and aspiration, as expressed through material depictions. The talk is presented by Kayleigh Danowski, Lois F. McNeil Fellow, Winterthur Program in American Material Culture. Registration required. Free.

A Nation Unraveled

During the American Civil War, clothing became central to the ways people waged war and experienced its cost. Through the clothes they made, wore, mended, lost, and stole, Americans expressed their allegiances, showed their love, confronted their social and economic challenges, subverted expectations, and, ultimately, preserved their history. As the collections they left behind make clear, Civil War Americans believed clothing was not merely a reflection of one’s class, gender, race, military rank, political ideology, or taste. Instead, Northerners and Southerners alike understood that clothing—from the weave of a fabric to the style and make of a coat—had the power to affect people’s way of living through the war’s tumult. In this lecture, Sarah Jones Weicksel discusses her new book, A Nation Unraveled: Clothing, Culture, and Violence in the American Civil War Era (University of North Carolina Press), a material history of war.

The Research at Winterthur series, presented by the Library, Research Fellowship Program, and Continuing Education, showcases new projects and publications that tap into our rich collections and resources, unveiling innovative perspectives for exploring the fascinating stories that objects can tell about people and our shared past. Registration required. Included with admission. Members free. Lecture followed by book signing.

America’s First Woman Botanist

Jane Colden (1724–1760) was America’s first woman botanist, yet her contributions to the field of remain little-known and her writings are mostly unpublished. Enjoy this lecture restoring Colden’s life and work, in her own writings, her father’s correspondence, and botanic sources of the 18th century with Fenella Greig Heckscher, author of Jane Colden’s Botanic Manuscript: The Legacy of America’s First Woman Botanist.

The Research at Winterthur series, presented by the Library, Research Fellowship Program, and Continuing Education, showcases new projects and publications that tap into our rich collections and resources, unveiling innovative perspectives for exploring the fascinating stories that objects can tell about people and our shared past. Registration required. Stitched in Place is a two-and-a-half-day conference that invites you to consider how place is not only a backdrop but a central thread in the story of American needlework. Join us to examine how Americans have used needlecraft and sewn and embroidered objects, whether stitched in schoolrooms, parlors, or workshops, to understand and communicate how they see the world and their places in it.

The conference will include research presentations, panel discussions, workshops for all interests and skill levels, special tours, and other exciting opportunities to engage with Winterthur’s extraordinary needlework collection.

Participants will see behind-the-scenes in the Needlework Study room, visit our Textile Conservation Lab, learn how Winterthur protects and preserves its collections, and learn about scalable ways to bring those practices into your own home and collections.
Registrants can sign up for a multiday workshop led by leading needle artists, learn more about our fantastic collections, and discover ways you can begin your own journeys of making and collecting.

Designed for a variety of audiences, Winterthur welcomes seasoned embroiderers, collectors, and those curious and eager to learn more. This conference draws its theme from an exhibit of the same name.

Stitched in Place, on view through April 4, 2027, explores how American needlework has and continues to serve as a medium for expressing identity, belonging, and awareness of place. Featuring approximately twenty objects from Winterthur’s collection, including  samplers, needlework pictures, hatchments, tools, garments, accessories, and furnishing textiles from the seventeenth through twentieth centuries, this installation invites reflection on how makers used needle and thread to communicate who they were, where they came from, and how they wished to be seen.
Stitched in Place is presented as part of Winterthur’s ongoing Conversations with Collections series in the Galleries.

• 70 hours of professional development in key skills and knowledge for cultural heritage study.
• support of the Winterthur learning community and a stronger professional network.

BOSCO BOISE OPEN STUDIO TOUR
ELI CRAVEN
October 10th | 10:00am – 6:00pm

free

Surel’s Place honors the legacy of artist Surel Mitchell (a founding member of BOSCO) by offering her home and studio to artists of promise, and of renown, for month-long residencies and professionally supported art events. In this inspiring live/work space, artists of all disciplines are given time and freedom to reflect, create, and share their work with the community. This year, Surel’s Place celebrates its 15th season, and will have Eli Craven in residence during the BOSCO Open Studios Tour.

Boise Open Studios Collective Organization features over 125 Treasure Valley artists working in painting, sculpture, photography, ceramics, printmaking, jewelry, textiles, mosaic, collage, assemblage, digital images, and glass. Their main event, the Open Studios Tour, occurs during the first two weekends of October each year, with half of the artists opening their studios on the first weekend and the rest on the second. This event aims to enhance public understanding of the artistic process, foster connections, and build community.

REGISTER

This collage workshop with Artist-in-Residence Eli Craven focuses on re-interpreting family image archives through alterations and combinations with additional found and made materials. We explore family photography and portraiture, the meanings they carry, and how we can transform them through these added materials. You may use additional materials such as thread, fabric, papers, documents, wood, mirrors, metals, etc. As we create collages and tell stories, we will also discuss the meaning behind the combinations of these materials and how images change over time.

You are encouraged to bring some of your own materials to work with: copies and test strips, in addition to originals of photographs intended to use in the workshop. A variety of found photographic images and various sources will also be available.
Partial scholarships available by request to info@surelsplace.org.

Although currently based in Indiana, Eli Craven was raised in Idaho. “Returning to Idaho for this project feels appropriate given the origins of my relationship to photography and a return to the subject matter of my childhood,” Eli says. In his childhood home, magazines and movies were censored, select films and TV shows were forbidden, sexuality and death were seldom discussed. The power images hold was discovered through scrutinizing forbidden magazine collections, daytime soap operas, and movies. The impetus of his practice resides in this desire to see, only to discover nothing shocking. Instead, seemingly mundane imagery is isolated and fragmented, presenting a narrative exploring the image’s role in processes of socialization.

Eli left Idaho with a BFA in photography from Boise State back in 2011. He went on to pursue an MFA in photography at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Currently an Associate Professor of Photography at Purdue University, his work has been widely exhibited and published. Most recently his work has been exhibited at Kant Gallery in Copenhagen, Denmark; KlompChing Gallery in Brooklyn, New York; and at the Blue Sky, Oregon Center for the Photographic Arts in Portland, Oregon.

EXHIBIT & ART TALK
A PLEA FOR TENDERNESS
Thursday, October 29th | 7:00pm – 8:30pm
free

In this project Eli Craven aims to position the viewer as a collaborator or partner in the physical experience of the work. Viewers are invited to alter photographic compositions through a series of kinetic elements and reflective materials, including sliding wood panels, hinged doors, and movable peepholes. The viewer must engage and activate the framing components to reveal the photographic image, potentially provoking the desire to see what is hidden within. Participation is integral to this project, with entire scenes rendered incomplete without the viewer’s touch and imagination filling the gaps and visualizing what lies beneath the surface of the photograph, or behind the veil.

Although the works exist within the canon of photography, they are sculptural objects that utilize the photograph as part of their construction. Eli’s work started with an obsession for photography and its materials and that fixation remains at the core of his practice.

[/et_pb_text][et_pb_accordion _builder_version=”4.27.0″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_accordion_item title=”October: Potion Power” open=”on” _builder_version=”4.27.0″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”]One Saturday session: October 31 | 1-5pm

This Halloween, enter a world of bubbling brews and mysterious mixtures as we uncover the real science behind classic potion-making! This month’s Pop-In Program uses a STEAM-focused approach to explore fizzy reactions, color-changing concoctions, and ingredients that behave in surprising ways. Participants will investigate the chemistry hidden inside spooky “witch’s brews” and magical transformations.

[/et_pb_accordion_item][et_pb_accordion_item title=”November: Pendulums! The Swing of Science” _builder_version=”4.27.0″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” open=”off”]Two Saturday sessions: November 7 & 28 | 1-5pm
The Swing of Science: Exploring the Power of the Pendulum

Discover how a simple swinging weight helped scientists understand motion, time, and the forces that shape our world! This month’s Pop-In Program uses a STEAM-focused approach to explore how pendulums move, what affects their swing, and why Galileo’s observations changed science forever. Participants will test different pendulum designs and experiment with patterns and timing.

[/et_pb_accordion_item][et_pb_accordion_item title=”December: It’s the Most Wonderful SLIME of the Year” _builder_version=”4.27.0″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” open=”off”]One Saturday session: December 5 | 1-5pm

Discover how a simple swinging weight helped scientists understand motion, time, and the forces that shape our world! This month’s Pop-In Program uses a STEAM-focused approach to explore how pendulums move, what affects their swing, and why Galileo’s observations changed science forever. A limited-time monthly series where kids search for clues and solve mysteries in the exhibits. Two sessions are available on the same Saturday each month: juniors ages 6 to 9, and detectives ages 10 to 13.
Petroglyph Wall: Mystery of the Ancestral Echoes

A cultural mystery is waiting to be uncovered. Join us as we explore Bailey Dann’s powerful artwork inspired by Shoshone-Bannock ancestral petroglyphs and stories passed down through generations. Kids will look closely at the shapes, figures, and patterns carved into the metal panels, consider how these markings help protect history, and imagine the echoes of stories carried through time. With the artist present to share her perspective, participants will gain a deeper understanding of how art continues the work of ancient story keepers!
Registration opens 30 days before each monthly session.

General admission is not included

James Jaxxa “What We Make Sacred”

James Jaxxa’s multi-faceted practice explores themes of memory, desire, vulnerability, community and pleasure through the creation of bedazzling personal reliquaries and cathartic shrines. His work is influenced from growing up nomadically in a military family, Catholic iconography and queer culture.

He received his MFA from the School of Visual Arts, his BS from Michigan State University and completed post-baccalaureate work at School of the Art Institute of Chicago and Rhode Island School of Design. He has attended residencies at Barac (Mannheim, Germany), Salzburg International Summer Academy (Salzburg, Austria), R.A.R.O. (Barcelona, Spain), Berlin Art Institute (Berlin, Germany) and others.

Jaxxa’s work has been shown in exhibitions across the United States and internationally including those at Terrain Biennial, New York Public Library, The LGBT Center in New York, University of Nevada, Newhouse Center for Contemporary Art, Seattle Art Museum, Bellevue Art Museum and numerous other institutions and galleries. His public artwork, Potential Connections was installed for the inauguration of Seattle’s Link Light Rail system. Jaxxa has been included in publications by The New York Times, Visual AIDS, New York Public Library and The Seattle Times. He was awarded an Artists Space Independent Project Grant.

Jaxxa is a founding member of I Found U, an international group of artists working across different materials and mediums, committed to discussion and collaboration on environmental, sociological and economic concerns. He lives and works in New York City.

Broadway Comes To Bradley II
October, 3, 2026 at 7:30pm in the Meyer Jacobs Theatre
For one night only… Broadway performer and Bradley University Theatre Arts Performance alum Morgan Siobhan Green, along with award-winning composer and lyricist Joe Iconis, are coming to Bradley!

After last year’s triumphant Broadway Comes to Bradley, in which Morgan performed alongside Tony and Pulitzer Prize winner Michael R. Jackson (A Strange Loop), we are thrilled to bring Morgan back again, along with another of her dear friends from the world of Broadway: composer and lyricist Joe Iconis.

Morgan was one of Bradley Theatre’s all-time best actors, excelled on BU’s Speech Team, and performed in Broadway’s Be More Chill and in the US National Tour of the smash-hit Broadway musical Hadestown.

Joe’s highly acclaimed musical Be More Chill was nominated for numerous Tony, Drama Desk, and Outer Critics Circle awards. This prolific artist has also written the music and lyrics for the musicals Broadway Bounty Hunter and Love in Hate Nation, and developed the musicals The Untitled Hunter S. Thompson Musical and Punk Rock Girl, among many other projects.
Morgan and Joe, along with Bradley’s Theatre Arts and Music students, will perform an evening of original music that is sure to delight and inspire.
Tickets can be purchased in-person at the Hartmann Center box office, or online.
Please join us for Broadway Comes to Bradley II – an exciting evening of music and fun!

Join the Illinois Cyber Foundation and the Center for Cybersecurity at Bradley University for BSides Peoria 2026, a one-day, community-driven cybersecurity conference bringing together professionals, students, educators, researchers and enthusiasts for a day of learning, hands-on exploration and collaboration.

Returning to Bradley on Saturday, Oct. 24, BSides Peoria features 15 technical talks, a dedicated keynote from Alethe Denis, hands-on villages, competitions and networking opportunities spanning a wide range of cybersecurity topics.

Attendees can explore the Physical Security Village, Human Hacking Village and Radio Frequency Village, with activities covering lockpicking and physical access controls, social engineering and human behavior, wireless technologies and RF security. Competitions include the BSides Peoria Capture the Flag, Vishing Challenge, Zero Trust, and Phish Bowl, offering opportunities for both experienced participants and newcomers to test their skills.

BSides events are built by the cybersecurity community, for the cybersecurity community, emphasizing accessible learning, conversation and participation. The Center for Cybersecurity has hosted BSides Peoria at Bradley University since the conference was established by the Illinois Cyber Foundation in 2023.

Whether you work in cybersecurity, are preparing to enter the field, or are simply curious about how technology can be attacked and defended, BSides Peoria offers opportunities to learn something new, meet others in the community and get hands-on with cybersecurity.

Registration is required. Visit BSidesPeoria.com for tickets, conference updates and additional information.

For the past 20 years, Bradley University’s Institute for Principled Leadership in Public Service has hosted a Women in Leadership luncheon honoring the legacy of Lydia Moss Bradley. This year’s luncheon, hosted by the Institute alongside the Peoria Women’s Club and Bradley President Jim Shadid, welcomes Kansas Governor Laura Kelly, a Bradley alumna, as the featured speaker. Governor Kelly is finishing her second and final four-year term and models the bipartisan, ethical, civil, and collaborative leadership approach the Institute promotes. James Jaxxa “What We Make Sacred”

James Jaxxa’s multi-faceted practice explores themes of memory, desire, vulnerability, community and pleasure through the creation of bedazzling personal reliquaries and cathartic shrines. His work is influenced from growing up nomadically in a military family, Catholic iconography and queer culture.

He received his MFA from the School of Visual Arts, his BS from Michigan State University and completed post-baccalaureate work at School of the Art Institute of Chicago and Rhode Island School of Design. He has attended residencies at Barac (Mannheim, Germany), Salzburg International Summer Academy (Salzburg, Austria), R.A.R.O. (Barcelona, Spain), Berlin Art Institute (Berlin, Germany) and others.

Jaxxa’s work has been shown in exhibitions across the United States and internationally including those at Terrain Biennial, New York Public Library, The LGBT Center in New York, University of Nevada, Newhouse Center for Contemporary Art, Seattle Art Museum, Bellevue Art Museum and numerous other institutions and galleries. His public artwork, Potential Connections was installed for the inauguration of Seattle’s Link Light Rail system. Jaxxa has been included in publications by The New York Times, Visual AIDS, New York Public Library and The Seattle Times. He was awarded an Artists Space Independent Project Grant.

Jaxxa is a founding member of I Found U, an international group of artists working across different materials and mediums, committed to discussion and collaboration on environmental, sociological and economic concerns. He lives and works in New York City.
